aspects.says: ConcurrentHashMap refuses null keys and values, so 'mapped to nothing' is stored as a sentinel or an Optional.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

aspects.says: ConcurrentHashMap.size() may be an approximation while other threads write.
aspects.reason: an approximation shows only under a race, which a deterministic test cannot force

aspects.says: ConcurrentHashMap's compute, merge and computeIfAbsent are atomic compound operations.
aspects.reason: atomicity shows only under contention, which a deterministic test cannot force; its single-threaded result is the same as a get-then-put

aspects.says: A CopyOnWriteArrayList iterator does not support remove(), which throws UnsupportedOperationException; the list's own remove or removeIf is used instead.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

aspects.says: CopyOnWriteArrayList suits read-heavy, write-rare work such as a listener registry.
basis: section:8.5.2.2. Fail-Safe Iterators and Snapshot Semantics

aspects.says: A CopyOnWriteArrayList iterator reads the array captured when it was created, so it never throws and never sees a later write.
basis: section:8.5.2.2. Fail-Safe Iterators and Snapshot Semantics

aspects.says: Each CopyOnWriteArrayList write copies the whole array, O(n), so writes are batched with addAll and write-heavy work uses another collection.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
aspects.reason: a cost a graded test cannot observe; asked on 8.5.3's quiz, which weighs it against a workload

aspects.says: Writing a HashMap from two threads without synchronization is undefined behaviour: lost updates or corrupted state, with no guaranteed exception.
aspects.reason: undefined behaviour under a race cannot be graded deterministically

aspects.says: The for-each loop runs on an iterator, so a change during it goes through the iterator's own methods, such as ListIterator.add(), which keeps the traversal in step.
A parallel stream over a fail-fast source must not modify it; results are collected into a new collection.
aspects.reason: practised on 8.5.3: 'Filter into a new list' collects instead of modifying its source

aspects.says: Only structural changes such as add, remove and clear move modCount; set() and put() on an existing key do not, so they do not trip a fail-fast iterator.
Collections.synchronizedList/Map/Set do not change the fail-fast contract, so iteration is synchronized on the wrapper.
aspects.reason: practised on 8.5.1: 'Traverse a synchronized list under its own lock' grades that the wrapper's lock is held

aspects.says: A ConcurrentHashMap iterator is weakly consistent: it never throws, returns each element at most once, and may or may not show writes made after it was created.
basis: section:8.5.2.2. Fail-Safe Iterators and Snapshot Semantics
